01

What this system is

The one-paragraph version, then the why.

Teams practising spec-driven development accumulate a folder of feature specs that is invisible in the tracker they actually live in. This system is an extension that closes that gap: install it into a repository and every feature folder is reflected into the team's tracker as structured issues, kept current automatically as work proceeds.

Two properties define its character. The sync is one-way — the repository is the source of truth and the tool never edits your files — and it works by reconciliation: each run reads the current state and converges the tracker toward it, rather than replaying a stream of events. A run against unchanged inputs makes no changes at all, which is what makes it idempotent and safe to repeat.

Core idea

The repository is the single source of truth for planned work; the tracker is a projection of it. The tool's job is to converge that projection toward the repository — idempotently, and without writing back to your files.

02

How you use it

The operator's view, before we open the hood.

Adding the system to a repository takes one input: a tracker API key. From the key alone the guided install discovers everything else — it verifies the key, lists the teams it can see as a numbered picker (auto-picking when there is only one), lists that team's projects with a create-new option, and writes the binding. The operator never sees or types an internal identifier.

Technical detail

The key is resolved before any tracker-aware step, then verified with a single identity query whose result is reused so identity is never fetched twice. The binding config is written before any hook wiring begins, and is retained even if a later wiring step fails; once the config exists the remaining wiring steps are independently rerunnable. (Hook registration itself is not promised to be atomic — an interruption partway can leave partial, rerunnable wiring.) (Earlier preparation — a key saved to a local env file, or a freshly created Project — may persist from an interrupted run; the guarantee is about config and hook wiring, not total atomicity.) A non-interactive path accepts pre-resolved identifiers as flags for automation.

Design choice — the API key is the only input

An earlier install required the operator to supply the tracker's internal identifiers up front — values its UI never shows. The current install inverts that: bring a key, and everything else is discovered for you.

03

Architecture at a glance

A reconcile engine over the filesystem, plus an optional real-time webhook.

The system reaches the tracker through two layers that converge on the same state from different angles. The reconcile layer reads the repository, computes what the tracker should contain, and makes it so — it is what every local trigger runs. A webhook layer fires on pull-request events and flips exactly one thing: a feature's workflow state when its pull request opens, becomes ready, or merges.

Technical detail

The reconcile layer alone is sufficient for correctness — it owns the full picture: labels, comments, sub-issues, descriptions, and project status. The webhook owns only the workflow-state flip, accelerating merges; it does not reconcile anything else, so it complements the reconcile layer rather than substituting for it. Both are idempotent. State lives only in the repository, the tracker, and the webhook's per-run environment — there is no database, no daemon, and no local cache of what the tracker last held, which is exactly what lets a fresh clone reconcile correctly.

04

The data model

How a feature folder maps onto the tracker.

The load-bearing decision of the whole system is a single mapping: a repository becomes one Project, each feature spec becomes one Issue inside it, each implementation phase becomes a sub-issue, and the tasks within a phase become a read-only checklist. A phase of work becomes a sub-issue; an individual task stays a checklist line — which keeps the tracker readable and the dependency graph small.

Technical detail

Ordering between phases is mirrored as blocking relations between sub-issues, and non-task artifacts — clarification rounds, plan summaries, findings — are surfaced as comments on the feature Issue. A feature advances along a fixed, ordered ladder of lifecycle phases inferred from filesystem state — which artifacts are present, plus implementation evidence on the branch and the pull request's open or merged state — each phase mapped to a tracker workflow state; the terminal merged phase is identified by its workflow state alone.

Unspecified — the ladder's exact ordering for drift comparison

The lifecycle ladder above is the full nine-phase sequence the bridge mirrors. A separate drift-comparison note ranks the phases in a slightly different, shorter order — swapping the two earliest and omitting the red-team and analysis phases. Because backward-drift turns on which phase outranks which, the canonical ordering for that comparison is not settled across the specifications; the full sequence is shown here and the discrepancy is flagged rather than resolved.

Technical detail

The fixed tracker bindings — the Project, the Team, and the nine workflow states — are held by immutable identifier rather than display name, so a rename in the tracker's UI cannot break a lookup; only deletion surfaces, as an explicit error. (Feature Issues and sub-issues are found by label instead — see Identity.)

Bind the workspace by identifier, not by name

The Project, Team, and workflow-state bindings use immutable identifiers because names are editable in the tracker's UI and a rename would silently break a name-based lookup. The only failure mode is deletion, which is surfaced explicitly rather than guessed around.

05

Components

Install, seed, and the single reconcile path.

The system installs into a repository through the spec-kit extension mechanism and auto-registers on the lifecycle hooks, so finishing a spec-kit command refreshes the tracker in the same step. A one-shot, re-runnable seed operation creates the labels and the nine workflow states the bridge needs in the workspace.

Technical detail

Every trigger — lifecycle hooks, git hooks, manual commands — routes through the one reconcile path, so behaviour is identical however a sync is started.

06

How work flows

Adoption, the everyday sync, and the real-time path.

The Project itself is established once, during install. On the first reconcile against an existing repository, the bridge enumerates every feature, infers each one's phase from its filesystem state — the artifacts present, plus implementation evidence on the branch and the pull request's state — and creates the matching Issues, sub-issues, checklists, and comments inside that Project. A feature already in a late phase such as merged converges directly to that terminal state without parading through every intermediate phase in the tracker's activity log.

Technical detail

In the everyday path, editing a single task and re-running changes exactly one line in exactly one sub-issue's checklist and nothing else. When a pull request merges, the webhook flips just that feature's workflow state within about a minute; if the webhook is absent, an ordinary reconcile flips it too — provided the merge is still detectable from the worktree (see the known gap under Boundaries when the branch has been deleted).

07

Identity & idempotency

Why running it twice is safe, with no local bookkeeping.

Idempotency rests on giving the per-feature tracker objects an identity the bridge can recompute from the filesystem, so it updates existing Issues and sub-issues instead of duplicating them — and it does this without keeping any local mapping file for them. (The fixed workspace bindings — Project, Team, workflow states — are a different matter: those identifiers are stored once in the committed config, as Components describes.)

Technical detail

A feature Issue is found by a workspace label scoped to the repository's Project, and a phase sub-issue by its parent plus a phase label. For a duplicate feature Issue from a race the bridge keeps the most-recently-active one and archives the rest; the data model describes sub-issue de-duplication only as analogous, without fully pinning down which copy is kept, so that finer rule is left slightly open. Because these dynamic identities are recomputed from filesystem-evident keys rather than stored, a sync from a fresh clone or any worktree resolves correctly.

No sidecar state — by principle

A local mapping file would drift across branches, worktrees, and clones. Recomputing identity from filesystem-evident keys instead is what lets a sync from a fresh clone, or any worktree, resolve correctly — and it is the same discipline that lets the reconciler need no cache of prior tracker state.

08

Authority & safety model

Who wins when the repository and the tracker disagree.

The governing principle is that the filesystem is the authority: when the repository and a tracker issue disagree, the repository wins — but never blindly. Any worktree may write, and before each write the bridge asks whether its view of a feature looks older than what the tracker already records.

Technical detail

That check, backward-drift, is computed from two inputs. The primary, semantic signal is lifecycle-phase ordering — drift fires when the tracker's recorded phase ranks higher than the phase inferred from disk. The corroborating signal is recency, comparing the spec directory's last commit time (never file modification time, which does not survive a clone) against the tracker's last-updated time within a small tolerance; recency reinforces but never raises drift on its own. Forward and equal movement never warn.

When drift is surfaced the operator decides — proceed and overwrite, or abort and leave the tracker untouched (an abort produces zero diff). The bridge never silently overwrites and never unilaterally refuses; detection is automatic and always on, but resolution belongs to the operator.

Surface, don't enforce

Detection is automatic and always on; resolution belongs to the operator. The bridge makes the risk visible and loud, but does not make the decision for you — which is what lets 'the filesystem wins' be safe to live with on a team.

Unspecified — does recency alone trigger drift?

The specifications disagree on whether the corroborating recency signal may raise drift by itself: the governing requirement says it must not (drift fires on phase ordering, with recency only reinforcing), while a companion design note frames the two signals as an either-or. This document follows the governing requirement; the disagreement is recorded here rather than silently resolved.

09

Decisions & evolution

The choices that shaped the system — including where it revised itself.

Write authority was redefined — branch-gate → drift-aware

Originally a hard branch-gate: only the worktree on a spec's own feature branch could write that spec to the tracker; every other worktree was read-only for it. Any worktree may write; before writing, the bridge detects backward-drift and surfaces it for the operator to resolve, rather than refusing. The filesystem — not the branch name — is the authority. The redesign spec frames the gate as too strict for merged specs (deleted branches), retroactive adoption, and trunk teams, and explicitly supersedes the earlier enforcement clause — a change significant enough to carry the project constitution from its first governing version to a second.

Install became key-only

The original install required the operator to supply the tracker's internal Team and Project identifiers up front — values the tracker's UI never displays. The operator brings only an API key; the install discovers team and project interactively and the operator never sees an internal identifier. The identifier-first path survives only as a non-interactive automation route. The install-ergonomics spec narrates the change in its overview as a direct response to operators being unable to find the identifiers the old flow demanded.

Technical detail

Other notable choices: map a task phase to a sub-issue and individual tasks to checklist lines, to keep the tracker readable; bind by immutable identifier; split sync into a reconcile layer and a webhook layer with disjoint write domains; and detect drift by phase ordering first, with git-commit recency as a clock-independent corroborator.

10

Boundaries & open questions

What the system does not settle.

By design the flow is one-way — the tracker is read to look issues up and to detect drift, never to update the files — and the bridge never mutates pull requests. The only removal the specs define is archiving a duplicate Issue produced by a race; a broader 'never deletes anything' guarantee is not something the specifications state. Several questions are genuinely unresolved in the specs and are recorded here rather than guessed at.

Known gap — merged features on a deleted branch

When a feature's pull request has merged and its branch is deleted, the merge can be hard to detect from another worktree, so the feature may show an earlier phase. The specs identify this as a concrete defect with a separately-recommended hardening follow-up, not a settled behaviour.

11

Where this is headed

What the specifications do — and do not — commit to.

Technical detail

The specifications describe the system as built for one tracker, and integrations beyond it are explicitly out of scope. Read this section narrowly: the architecture is organized around a single mapping from repository concepts to that tracker's primitives, and that is the whole of what the specs commit to. No second destination, and no general multi-destination engine, is defined.

Unspecified — additional destinations

Whether the engine is ever pointed at a second tracker or output is not addressed by these specifications; the current tracker is the only destination they define.
